subject: physics
question_text: Distinguish between conservative and non-conservative forces with one example each.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 6 SHORT ANSWER. The mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed, so appearances[] stays empty. The TSBIE Basic Learning Material has no SAQ section for this unit, so the Fastrack is the only source for it. AI physics check 2026-08-24: formulas, signs, numbers and claims verified against NCERT Class-11 conventions; corrections applied to explanation text (why / common_mistakes / memory_tip), marked answer lines unchanged unless factually wrong.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Conservative forces
lines: 1. The work done around a closed path
2. The work done is independent of the

lines.text: path — it depends only on the end

steps.margin_note: Number the points and put the example last. A "distinguish" question is marked point by point.
steps.why: Both properties are the same fact twice: if the work back is exactly minus the work out, going round a loop must give zero.
common_mistakes: Writing prose instead of numbered points, so the matching pairs cannot be seen.

recall.must_convey: That for a conservative force the work in a closed path is zero and is path-independent, e.g. gravity.
accept: work in a closed path is zero
work is independent of the path

steps.memory_tip: Two marks, two properties: work is path-independent, and work round a closed loop is zero. Example: gravity.

steps.label: Non-conservative forces
lines: 1. The work done around a closed path
2. The work done depends on the path
steps.margin_note: Answer point 1 against point 1 and point 2 against point 2 — the same order as the column beside it.
steps.why: Friction always opposes the motion, so it takes energy on the way out AND on the way back. A longer path costs more, which is exactly what path-dependent means.
common_mistakes: Giving a different number of points on the two sides, so nothing lines up.

recall.must_convey: That for a non-conservative force the closed-path work is not zero and depends on the path, e.g. friction.
accept: work in a closed path is not zero
reject: work in a closed path is zero

steps.memory_tip: Friction is the example to name: it opposes the motion BOTH ways, so a longer path costs more.

steps.label: The energy difference
lines: A conservative force stores energy that
can be recovered, so a potential energy
can be defined for it. A non-conservative
force dissipates energy as heat, so no
steps.margin_note: Unmarked, but it is the reason behind both columns. Write it if there is room.
steps.why: This is the useful half of the distinction: it tells you when you are allowed to use mgh or ½kx² at all.
common_mistakes: Claiming friction has a potential energy.
Thinking every non-conservative force removes energy. A push from a hand is also non-conservative and can add energy; the real point is that its work cannot be stored as a potential energy.

recall.must_convey: That a potential energy can be defined for a conservative force but not for a non-conservative one.
accept: potential energy can be defined only for conservative forces
conservative force ki potential energy untundi

steps.memory_tip: The useful line: only conservative forces store energy you can get back — that is when mgh and ½kx² exist.
